I am a 68-year-old man, and I have farmed this land in Quzhou since I was a boy. My father taught me everything I know; I never went to school, but I know this soil and this weather better than any book. We have six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. Every year I plant the same thing because it works: winter wheat in the autumn, and then summer maize right after the wheat comes off in June. That is how we have always done it here. The wheat feeds us, and the maize brings in cash and feeds the pigs. I buy my wheat seed from the local supply shop — the improved kind, not the old traditional grain, because it yields better but I do not trust those fancy new names. For maize I buy hybrid seed; everyone does, and the ears are big. I till the land with the rotary tiller before I sow the wheat to break up the stubble, but when the wheat is cut, there is no time to waste — I plant the maize directly into the field without ploughing. I put down fertilizer the way I have always done: plenty of nitrogen to make the crops green and tall, some phosphorus, and a bit of potassium. I know the young technicians say I use too much, but when I cut back, my yields drop, and I cannot afford that risk at my age. I irrigate from the well four times for the wheat — winter water, jointing, heading, and filling — and three times for the maize when it is silking and grain-filling. I spray when I see insects or when the shop man tells me others are spraying. I expect about 500 jin per mu for wheat and around 550 jin per mu for maize in a normal year, God willing.
